newsitem.title: UK: Italian bonds to draw no comfort from budget.
newsitem.headline: Italian bonds to draw no comfort from budget.

text.p: Italy's supplementary budget plans, designed to help its campaign to join European monetary union, are being treated as a paper-shuffling exercise and will leave Italian government bonds vulnerable, analysts said on Thursday.
Some analysts say a widespread bear market is starting for bonds, in which Italian BTPs will suffer.
Some forecasts predict the gap between the yield of BTPs and German Bunds will widen as far as 230 basis points, or 2.3 percentage points, in the months ahead.
"There are no real budget measures included," said Lorenzo Codogno, head of economics and market research in Milan before Prime Minister Romano Prodi's cabinet approved its well-trailed mini-budget.
The measure, which has met widespread criticism for only being a stop-gap attempt to win Italy entry to the single European currency, includes 15.5 trillion lire ($9.2 billion) of deficit cuts.
"It's nothing compared to what is really needed to prepare the Italian economy for EMU (European economic and monetary union). It could only disappoint our partners," Codogno said.
His was not a lone view.
"I haven't seen any comment where anyone is suggesting these measures can be seen as anything but dubious," said Adrian Schmidt, interantional economist at Chase in London.
Schmidt saw less downside for BTPs than other analysts but that was not because of Italy's fiscal plans. "I don't think the mini-budget can be seen as positive in any shape or form."

The spread between Italy's 7.75 percent BTP due in November 1996 and the 6.0 percent January 1997 Bund was 187 basis points at 1105 GMT. It has edged up from the low 140s in late January, although in the past couple of weeks it has narrowed sharply from more than 215.
Analysts said one big reason why the spread was likely to widen was that with European growth starting to pick up, the Bank of Italy's room to cut interest rates was diminishing.
"Even with very good inflation numbers it's becoming very difficult for Italy to cut rates," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. "The budget doesn't help."
Giordano said the BTP/Bund gap could widen out to 230 basis points, a target he shared with Codogno, who believes that could happen on a one to three month basis.

"There is a clear perception that we have turned the interest rate cycle. We are in the middle of a bear market, so it's rather unlikely that Italy will outperform in this situation," he said. "We might see a gradual deterioration of the spread. I'm not expecting a selloff but clearly we will remain weak."

Schmidt, however, disagreed that a bear market was definitely underway. He also argued that considering the amount of talk there has been about a delay to EMU in recent weeks, BTPs have held up fairly well.

"It (the BTP spread) has actually moved a lot less than you would have expected. For that reason I think there's limited downside unless we get some solid evidence of a delay." He added, "I would doubt we'll see EMU delay fears increase that much." ($ = 1677 Italian Lire)
